before: Prosperity teaching, sometimes called the "health and wealth gospel" or "prosperity gospel," holds that God wants every believer to be physically healthy and financially rich in this life, and that faith, positive confession and giving to the ministry will bring this about. It takes many forms, and not everyone who teaches some of it teaches all of it.
after: In this unit, “prosperity teaching” refers to forms of Christian teaching that promise health and material increase to believers through faith, confession, or giving. The term covers a range of teachings and should not be applied to a person or church without examining its actual claims. Distinguish extreme transactional promises from broader Pentecostal teaching that God provides, heals, and blesses, while also recognizing biblical warnings about greed and financial exploitation.

before: It has several roots. E. W. Kenyon, a writer of the early twentieth century, taught about the power of faith-filled words. Kenneth Hagin, who began as a Pentecostal preacher, spread similar ideas in the "Word of Faith" movement. Oral Roberts, a Pentecostal healing evangelist, taught "seed faith," the idea that a gift given to God is a seed that returns with increase. David Yonggi Cho, whom we met in Unit 8, taught a "threefold blessing" of salvation, health and prosperity, based on 3 John 2. Later the message spread through television, books and large churches. It now has many forms in North America, Africa, Latin America and Asia. The Universal Church of the Kingdom of God, mentioned in Unit 9, is one well-known example in Brazil.

before: The problem is that prosperity teaching turns these truths into a formula, promises wealth and health to all who follow the formula, and sets money at the center of the Christian life. We reject it for the following reasons.
after: The problem, as this course understands it, is the use of faith, confession, or giving as a transaction that guarantees health or wealth, especially when sickness or poverty is blamed on the believer or money is directed to an unaccountable leader. Evaluate specific teachings and practices rather than assigning this description to every Pentecostal teacher who speaks of God’s provision. We reject it for the following reasons.

before: Classical Pentecostal denominations and leaders in many countries have warned against the extreme forms of this teaching, and other evangelicals have as well. An international consultation of evangelical leaders in Ghana in 2009, with the Lausanne Movement, studied the subject, and a statement from the Lausanne Theology Working Group followed in 2010. We hold that "full gospel" teaching centers on Jesus as Savior, Healer, Baptizer with the Spirit and Coming King, and must be kept separate from a gospel of success.

before: Early Pentecostals were often rejected by other churches, and they responded by separating. In the later twentieth century this began to change. The first World Pentecostal Conference met in Zurich in 1947. In the United States, the Assemblies of God took part in the founding of the National Association of Evangelicals in 1943. In 1961 two Chilean Pentecostal bodies joined the World Council of Churches, which was unusual among Pentecostals. As we saw in Unit 9, David du Plessis worked to build bridges, and formal talks between Pentecostals and the Roman Catholic Church began in 1972.
